name: Glow Protocol

lead: Glow Protocol is an online peptide blend, usually GHK-Cu plus BPC-157 and TB-500, marketed for skin glow and recovery.
Users look to it for firmer, brighter skin, citing GHK-Cu's collagen research.

angle.text: People use the blend hoping for a firmer, brighter complexion. The reasoning rests on GHK-Cu's collagen research and on repair studies of the other two peptides.

lead: Glow Protocol, also sold as the GLOW blend, is a vendor-assembled peptide blend marketed online for skin quality. The usual listing combines GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in one vial, with a common split of about 50 mg, 10 mg and 10 mg.[1][2] Some sellers list variants that add other peptides such as KPV.[2]

Users take it for a lit-from-within, firmer-looking complexion and faster recovery, drawing on GHK-Cu's association with collagen and wound-repair research.[1] Vendors label it research use only.[1][2]
Research on the individual peptides is mostly in cells and animals. No published human study has tested the three-peptide combination.[1]
infobox: Sold as research use only; not approved as a drug or cosmetic[1]

paras: Most listings describe GHK-Cu (about 50 mg), BPC-157 (about 10 mg) and TB-500 (about 10 mg).[1][2] GHK-Cu is a copper-binding peptide studied for wound repair and collagen production; BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide studied in animals for tendon, gut and wound healing; TB-500 is a synthetic peptide based on thymosin beta-4, studied in animals for wound closure.[1] Contents differ between sellers.[2]

The blend is not approved by the FDA as a drug or cosmetic. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee reviewed BPC-157 and TB-500 on whether licensed pharmacies may compound them, and FDA staff noted limited quality, safety and effectiveness data for BPC-157.[1]
No studies found. Research on GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 individually is mostly in cells and animals and concerns healing after injury.[1]
